claim: We read jumbled words effortlessly.
source: We read jubmled wrods effortlessly, but the neural correlates of this remarkable ability remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the Cambridge University effect example in the manuscript.

claim: The neural correlates of jumbled word reading remain poorly understood.
source: We read jubmled wrods effortlessly, but the neural correlates of this remarkable ability remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Viewing a jumbled word activates a visual representation that is compared to known words.
source: We hypothesized that viewing a jumbled word activates a visual representation that is compared to known words.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Neurons tuned to letter shape can respond to longer strings in a compositional manner by linearly summing letter responses.
source: To test this hypothesis, we devised a purely visual model in which neurons tuned to letter shape respond to longer strings in a compositional manner by linearly summing letter responses.
evidence: This describes the computational model developed and tested in the study.

claim: Dissimilarities between letter strings in the compositional model can explain human performance on visual search.
source: We found that dissimilarities between letter strings in this model can explain human performance on visual search, and responses to jumbled words in word reading tasks.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Dissimilarities between letter strings in the compositional model can explain responses to jumbled words in word reading tasks.
source: We found that dissimilarities between letter strings in this model can explain human performance on visual search, and responses to jumbled words in word reading tasks.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the word reading experiments.

claim: Viewing a string activates a letter-based code in the lateral occipital (LO) region.
source: Brain imaging revealed that viewing a string activates this letter-based code in the lateral occipital (LO) region and that subsequent comparisons to stored words are consistent with activations of the visual word form area (VWFA).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data showing neural dissimilarities in LO match perceptual dissimilarities.

claim: Subsequent comparisons to stored words are consistent with activations of the visual word form area (VWFA).
source: Brain imaging revealed that viewing a string activates this letter-based code in the lateral occipital (LO) region and that subsequent comparisons to stored words are consistent with activations of the visual word form area (VWFA).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data showing VWFA activity correlates with lexical decision times.

claim: A compositional neural code potentially contributes to efficient reading.
source: Thus, a compositional neural code potentially contributes to efficient reading.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined behavioral and neuroimaging results.

claim: Word reading can be influenced by visual, phonological and linguistic processing.
source: Reading a word or a jumbled word can be influenced by a variety of factors such as visual, phonological and linguistic processing (Norris, 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Word reading is easy when similar shapes are substituted.
source: At the visual level, word reading is easy when similar shapes are substituted (Perea et al., 2008; Perea and Panadero, 2014), when the first and last letters are preserved (Rayner et al., 2006), when there are fewer transpositions (Gomez et al., 2008), when word shape is preserved (Norris, 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Word reading is easy when the first and last letters are preserved.
source: At the visual level, word reading is easy when similar shapes are substituted (Perea et al., 2008; Perea and Panadero, 2014), when the first and last letters are preserved (Rayner et al., 2006), when there are fewer transpositions (Gomez et al., 2008), when word shape is preserved (Norris, 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Word reading is easy when there are fewer transpositions.
source: At the visual level, word reading is easy when similar shapes are substituted (Perea et al., 2008; Perea and Panadero, 2014), when the first and last letters are preserved (Rayner et al., 2006), when there are fewer transpositions (Gomez et al., 2008), when word shape is preserved (Norris, 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Word reading is easy when word shape is preserved.
source: At the visual level, word reading is easy when similar shapes are substituted (Perea et al., 2008; Perea and Panadero, 2014), when the first and last letters are preserved (Rayner et al., 2006), when there are fewer transpositions (Gomez et al., 2008), when word shape is preserved (Norris, 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is easier to read frequent words.
source: At the linguistic level, it is easier to read frequent words, words with frequent bigrams or trigrams as well as shuffled words that preserve intermediate units such as consonant clusters or morphemes (Norris, 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It is easier to read words with frequent bigrams or trigrams.
source: At the linguistic level, it is easier to read frequent words, words with frequent bigrams or trigrams as well as shuffled words that preserve intermediate units such as consonant clusters or morphemes (Norris, 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It is easier to read shuffled words that preserve intermediate units such as consonant clusters or morphemes.
source: At the linguistic level, it is easier to read frequent words, words with frequent bigrams or trigrams as well as shuffled words that preserve intermediate units such as consonant clusters or morphemes (Norris, 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: OFRGET is easy to find among FORGET in visual search.
source: It can be seen that finding OFRGET is easy among FORGET, whereas finding FOGRET is hard (Figure 1B), showing that FOGRET is more visually similar to FORGET.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1B showing visual search arrays.

claim: FOGRET is hard to find among FORGET in visual search.
source: It can be seen that finding OFRGET is easy among FORGET, whereas finding FOGRET is hard (Figure 1B), showing that FOGRET is more visually similar to FORGET.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1B showing visual search arrays.

claim: FOGRET is more visually similar to FORGET than OFRGET is.
source: It can be seen that finding OFRGET is easy among FORGET, whereas finding FOGRET is hard (Figure 1B), showing that FOGRET is more visually similar to FORGET.
evidence: This is inferred from the visual search difficulty shown in Figure 1B.

claim: FOGRET is easy to recognize as FORGET compared to OFRGET.
source: This makes FOGRET easy to recognize as FORGET compared to OFRGET.
evidence: This is inferred from the visual similarity relationship.

claim: Visual similarity of jumbled words to the original word potentially explains why transposing middle letters renders a word easier to read than transposing edge letters.
source: Thus, the visual similarity of the jumbled words FOGRET and OFRGET to the original word FORGET (Figure 1C) potentially explains why transposing the middle letters renders a word easier to read than transposing its edge letters.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the visual search example.

claim: Orthographic processing can potentially be explained by purely visual processing without invoking any linguistic factors.
source: This example suggests that orthographic processing can potentially be explained by purely visual processing (as indexed by visual search) without invoking any linguistic factors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the visual search example.

claim: Perceptually similar images elicit similar activity in single neurons.
source: First, perceptually similar images elicit similar activity in single neurons (Op de Beeck et al., 2001; Sripati and Olson, 2010a; Zhivago and Arun, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neurophysiology studies.

claim: The neural response to multiple objects is an average of the individual object responses.
source: Second, the neural response to multiple objects is an average of the individual object responses (Zoccolan et al., 2005; Ghose and Maunsell, 2008; Zhivago and Arun, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neurophysiology studies.

claim: Neurons in high-level visual cortex are tuned for letter shape and retinal position.
source: Our model only assumes neurons tuned for letter shape and retinal position, as observed in high-level visual cortex (Lehky and Tanaka, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous neurophysiology study.

claim: Subjects were highly consistent in their responses in Experiment 1.
source: Subjects were highly consistent in their responses (split-half correlation between average search times of odd- and even-numbered subjects: r = 0.87, p<0.00005).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Letter dissimilarities from visual search were significantly correlated with previously reported subjective dissimilarity ratings.
source: These letter dissimilarities were significantly correlated with previously reported subjective dissimilarity ratings (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis with previous data.

claim: Shape dissimilarity in visual search matches closely with neural dissimilarity in visual cortex.
source: Since shape dissimilarity in visual search matches closely with neural dissimilarity in visual cortex (Sripati and Olson, 2010a; Zhivago and Arun, 2014), we asked whether these letter distances can be used to reconstruct the underlying neural responses to single letters.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The first dimension of the MDS analysis represents the activity of a neuron that responds strongest to the letter O and weakest to X.
source: For example, the first dimension represents the activity of a neuron that responds strongest to the letter O and weakest to X (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C based on MDS analysis of visual search data.

claim: The second dimension of the MDS analysis corresponds to a neuron that responds strongest to L and weakest to E.
source: Likewise the second dimension corresponds to a neuron that responds strongest to L and weakest to E (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C based on MDS analysis of visual search data.

claim: Increasing the number of MDS dimensions led to increased match to the observed letter dissimilarities.
source: As expected, increasing the number of MDS dimensions led to increased match to the observed letter dissimilarities (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D based on MDS analysis.

claim: Letter transpositions are more similar compared to letter substitutions in visual search.
source: It can be seen that, finding TA among AT is harder than finding UT among AT. Thus, letter transpositions are more similar compared to letter substitutions, consistent with the classic results on reading (Norris, 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Subjects were highly consistent in their performance in Experiment 2.
source: As before, subjects were highly consistent in their performance (split-half correlation between odd and even-numbered subjects across all bigrams: r = 0.82, p<0.00005).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The letter model yielded excellent fits to the observed bigram search data (r = 0.85, p<0.00005).
source: This letter model yielded excellent fits to the observed data (r = 0.85, p<0.00005; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The letter model captured nearly all the systematic variance in the bigram search data.
source: This consistency measure (rdata = 0.90) was close to the model fit, suggesting that the model captured nearly all the systematic variance in the data.
evidence: This is based on comparison of model fit to data consistency.

claim: The estimated spatial summation weights were unequal.
source: As predicted in the schematic figure (Figure 3B), the estimated spatial summation weights were unequal (absolute difference between w1 and w2, mean ± sd: 0.07 ± 0.04).
evidence: This is based on parameter estimation from the model fitting.

claim: The absolute difference between spatial summation weights was significantly larger than for shuffled weights.
source: The absolute difference between shuffled weights was significantly smaller than for the original weights (average absolute difference: 0.03 ± 0.02; p<0.005, sign-rank test across 10 neurons).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison with shuffled control data.

claim: Model errors are not systematically different for frequent compared to infrequent bigram pairs.
source: This too revealed no systematic difference (mean ± sd of residual error: 0.10 ± 0.08 for the 20 most frequent bigrams and words; 0.11 ± 0.09 for 20 least frequent bigrams; p=0.80, rank-sum test).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model errors.

claim: Bigram search can be explained entirely using single neurons tuned to single letters.
source: We conclude that bigram search can be explained entirely using single neurons tuned to single letters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: The response to transposed bigrams such as AB and BA will be different only if the summation weights are unequal.
source: As detailed earlier, a critical prediction of this model is that the response to transposed bigrams such as AB and BA will be different only if the summation weights are unequal.
evidence: This is a logical prediction from the model structure.

claim: Repeated letter bigrams such as AA and BB will remain discriminable regardless of the nature of summation.
source: By contrast, repeated letter bigrams such as AA and BB will remain discriminable regardless of the nature of summation, since their response will be proportional to the respective single letter responses.
evidence: This is a logical prediction from the model structure.

claim: Familiarity might modulate the summation to make it more asymmetric.
source: Since reading expertise can modulate sensitivity to letter transpositions, we reasoned that familiarity might modulate the summation to make it more asymmetric.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning about reading expertise.

claim: Transposed letter searches will be easier to discriminate in a familiar upright orientation compared to the unfamiliar inverted orientation.
source: We therefore predicted that this would make transposed letter searches (with AB as target and BA as distractor, or vice-versa) easier to discriminate in a familiar upright orientation compared to the (unfamiliar) inverted orientation.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the familiarity hypothesis.

claim: Searches involving repeated letter bigrams will remain equally easy in both upright and inverted orientations.
source: By contrast, searches involving repeated letter bigrams (with AA as target and BB as distractor), which also have a change in two letters, will remain equally easy in both upright and inverted orientations.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model structure.

claim: Subjects discriminated repeated letter bigrams (AA-BB searches) equally well at both upright and inverted orientations.
source: As predicted, subjects discriminated repeated letter bigrams (AA-BB searches) equally well at both upright and inverted orientations, but were substantially faster at discriminating transposed letter pairs (AB-BA searches) in the upright orientation (Figure 3D; for detailed analyses see Appendix 2).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Subjects were substantially faster at discriminating transposed letter pairs (AB-BA searches) in the upright orientation compared to inverted.
source: As predicted, subjects discriminated repeated letter bigrams (AA-BB searches) equally well at both upright and inverted orientations, but were substantially faster at discriminating transposed letter pairs (AB-BA searches) in the upright orientation (Figure 3D; for detailed analyses see Appendix 2).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a larger difference in the model summation weights for upright compared to inverted bigrams.
source: Correspondingly, we observed a larger difference in the model summation weights for upright compared to inverted bigrams (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on model parameter estimation shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Familiarity leads to asymmetric spatial summation.
source: We conclude that familiarity leads to asymmetric spatial summation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the upright vs inverted bigram results.

claim: The single letter model yielded excellent fits to the six-letter string visual search data.
source: The single letter model yielded excellent fits to the data (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the behavioral data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The letter model fits were superior to the Orthographic Levenshtein Distance (OLD) model.
source: These fits were superior to a widely used measure of string similarity, the Orthographic Levenshtein Distance (OLD) model (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on model comparison shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The letter model fits were equivalent for both word-word pairs and nonword-nonword pairs.
source: Importantly, the letter model fits were equivalent for both word-word pairs and nonword-nonword pairs (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is based on model fitting analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Response times for nonwords will be inversely proportional to word frequency.
source: We also predict that this comparison will be affected by the strength of the stored word representation, such that matches to frequent words are easier. In other words, we predict that response times for nonwords will be inversely proportional to word frequency.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model.

claim: When viewing the string 'PENCIL', the match to the stored word PENCIL takes no time and the response is dominated by word frequency.
source: Finally, by the same account, when we view the string 'PENCIL', the match to the stored word PENCIL takes no time (the distance being negligible) and the response is therefore dominated by word frequency.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model.

claim: Subjects were highly accurate in responding to both words and nonwords in Experiment 5.
source: Subjects were highly accurate in responding to both words and nonwords (mean ± sd: 96 ± 2% for words, 95 ± 3% for nonwords).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from Experiment 5.

claim: Response times across words and nonwords were consistent between subjects in Experiment 5.
source: Importantly, their response times across words and nonwords were consistent between subjects as evidenced by a significant split-half correlation (correlation between odd- and even-numbered subjects: r = 0.59 for words, r = 0.73 for nonwords, p<0.00005).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Response times for words showed a negative correlation with log word frequency (r = −0.5, p<0.00005).
source: As predicted, response times for words showed a negative correlation with log word frequency (r = −0.5, p<0.00005 across 450 words).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Word frequency is the best predictor of word response times.
source: It can be seen that the word frequency is the best predictor of word response times (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on cross-validated model comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The combined lexical model performance was slightly better than the performance of the word frequency model alone.
source: To assess whether all lexical factors together predict word response times any better, we fit a combined model in which the word response times are modeled as a linear sum of the four factors. The combined model performance was slightly better than the performance of the word frequency model alone (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on cross-validated model comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Word response times are determined primarily by word frequency and to a lesser degree by letter frequency.
source: We conclude that word response times are determined primarily by word frequency and to a lesser degree by letter frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: The dependence of word response times on word frequency is non-compositional.
source: We note that the dependence of word response times on word frequency is non-compositional, since it cannot be explained by letter frequency.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model results.

claim: The letter model yielded excellent fits to the nonword response time data (r = 0.70, p<0.00005).
source: This model yielded excellent fits to the data (r = 0.70, p<0.00005; Figure 4E) that were comparable to the data consistency (rdata = 0.84).
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Subjects took longer to respond to nonwords obtained by transposing a letter of a word, compared to nonwords obtained through letter substitution.
source: Specifically, subjects took longer to respond to nonwords obtained by transposing a letter of a word, compared to nonwords obtained through letter substitution – these trends were present in the model predictions as well (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data and model predictions shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Subjects took longer when the middle letters were transposed compared to when the edge letters were transposed.
source: Likewise, subjects took longer when the middle letters were transposed compared to when the edge letters were transposed – as did the model predictions (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data and model predictions shown in Figure 4F.

claim: These effects replicate the classic orthographic processing effects reported across many studies.
source: These effects replicate the classic orthographic processing effects reported across many studies (Grainger et al., 2012; Norris, 2013; Ziegler et al., 2013; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The OLD model yielded relatively poorer predictions of the nonword data (r = 0.36, p<0.00005).
source: The OLD model yielded relatively poorer predictions of the data (r = 0.36, p<0.00005; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on model fitting shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The letter model outperformed both the OLD model and the lexical model in predicting nonword response times.
source: The letter model outperformed both the OLD model and the lexical model (model correlations: r = 0.56 ± 0.02, 0.33 ± 0.01 and 0.35 ± 0.01 for the neural, OLD and lexical models; fraction of bootstrap samples with neural <other models: p<0.005; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on cross-validated model comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The reduced SID model yielded fits that were better than the lexical model.
source: Even this reduced model yielded fits were better than the lexical model (SID model correlation: r = 0.48 ± . 02).
evidence: This is based on cross-validated model comparison.

claim: The model trained on visual search data yielded a significant positive correlation with nonword response times (r = 0.39, p<0.00005).
source: To assess whether the model trained on visual search data would also be able to predict nonword response times, we took the model trained on the visual search data in Experiment 4, and calculated the word-nonword distances using this model. This too yielded a significant positive correlation (r = 0.39, p<0.00005) that was better than the OLD and lexical models.
evidence: This is based on cross-experiment model generalization.

claim: A combined neural+lexical model explained more variance than either model alone.
source: Finally, a combined model – in which the neural and lexical model predictions were linearly combined – proved to explain more variance than either model (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on model comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Word response times are explained primarily by word frequency.
source: In sum, we conclude that word response times are explained primarily by word frequency and nonword response times are explained primarily by the distance between the nonword and the nearest word calculated using the compositional neural code.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lexical decision task results.

claim: Nonword response times are explained primarily by the distance between the nonword and the nearest word calculated using the compositional neural code.
source: In sum, we conclude that word response times are explained primarily by word frequency and nonword response times are explained primarily by the distance between the nonword and the nearest word calculated using the compositional neural code.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lexical decision task results.

claim: The perceptual and semantic dissimilarities were uncorrelated (r = 0.03, p=0.55).
source: Importantly, the perceptual and semantic dissimilarities were uncorrelated (r = 0.03, p=0.55), thereby allowing us to identify regions with distinct or overlapping perceptual/semantic representations.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between perceptual and semantic dissimilarity measures.

claim: Subjects were highly accurate in the fMRI lexical decision task (mean ±std of accuracy: 94 ± 4%).
source: Subjects were highly accurate (mean ±std of accuracy: 94 ± 4%) and showed consistent response time variations (split-half correlation between odd and even subjects: rsh = 0.54 and 0.79 for words and nonwords, p<0.00005).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from Experiment 6.

claim: Subjects showed consistent response time variations in the fMRI lexical decision task.
source: Subjects were highly accurate (mean ±std of accuracy: 94 ± 4%) and showed consistent response time variations (split-half correlation between odd and even subjects: rsh = 0.54 and 0.79 for words and nonwords, p<0.00005).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The lexical decision time for words was negatively correlated with word frequency (r = −0.42, p<0.05) in the fMRI experiment.
source: As before, the lexical decision time for words was negatively correlated with word frequency (r = −0.42, p<0.05).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the behavioral data from Experiment 6.

claim: The lexical decision times for nonwords were strongly correlated with the word-nonword dissimilarity measured in visual search (r = −0.68, p<0.00005).
source: Likewise, the lexical decision times for nonwords were strongly correlated with the word-nonword dissimilarity measured in visual search in Experiment 7 (r = −0.68, p<0.00005).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between Experiments 6 and 7.

claim: VWFA and TG regions showed greater activation to nonwords compared to words.
source: While V4 showed greater activation for words compared to nonwords, VWFA and TG regions showed greater activation to nonwords compared to words, presumably reflecting greater engagement to discriminate nonwords that are highly similar to words (Appendix 7).
evidence: This is based on fMRI activation analysis.

claim: Only the LO dissimilarities showed a significant correlation with perceptual dissimilarities (r = 0.16, p<0.00005).
source: Among the ROIs tested, only the LO dissimilarities showed a significant correlation (correlation between 1024 pairwise dissimilarities involving 32C2 words, 32C2 nonwords, and 32 word-nonword pairs: r = 0.16, p<0.00005; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between neural and perceptual dissimilarities shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A searchlight analysis confirmed that the match to perceptual dissimilarities was strongest in a region centred around the bilateral LO region.
source: A searchlight analysis confirmed that the match to perceptual dissimilarities was strongest in a region centred around the bilateral LO region (Appendix 7).
evidence: This is based on searchlight analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: LO is the likely neural substrate for the compositional letter code.
source: Thus, neural dissimilarity in the LO region match best with the perceptual dissimilarities observed in visual search. We therefore conclude that LO is the likely neural substrate for the compositional letter code.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural dissimilarity analysis.

claim: The match to semantic space was significant only in the LO and TG regions.
source: The match to semantic space was significant only in the LO and TG regions (correlation between 496 pairwise dissimilarities between words: r = 0.18 ± 0.05 for LO, 0.22 ± 0.04 for TG; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between neural and semantic dissimilarities shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A searchlight analysis confirmed that semantic dissimilarities were best correlated with the TG region.
source: A searchlight analysis confirmed that semantic dissimilarities were best correlated with the TG region with additional peaks in prefrontal and motor regions (Appendix 7).
evidence: This is based on searchlight analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: There is no significant difference between the neural representation in LO matching with perceptual or semantic space for word-word pairs.
source: This revealed no significant difference between the two correlations (r = 0.16 ± . 04 for LO with visual search, r = 0.16 ± 0.05 for LO with semantic dissimilarites; p=0.49 across 1000 bootstrap samples).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of correlations.

claim: Both LO and TG regions represent semantic space.
source: We conclude that both LO and TG regions represent semantic space.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the semantic dissimilarity analysis.

claim: Only the VWFA showed a consistently positive correlation with lexical decision times for both words and nonwords.
source: Across the ROIs, only the VWFA showed a consistently positive correlation with lexical decision times for both words and nonwords (r = 0.52, p<0.005 for words; r = 0.47, p<0.05 for nonwords, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between VWFA activity and lexical decision times shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A searchlight analysis confirmed that there was a peak in the correlation with lexical decision times centred on the VWFA.
source: A searchlight analysis confirmed that there was indeed a peak in the correlation with lexical decision times centred on the VWFA, with additional peaks in the parietal and frontal regions (Appendix 7).
evidence: This is based on searchlight analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: VWFA activations were larger for nonwords compared to words.
source: Interestingly, VWFA activations were larger for nonwords compared to words (mean ± std of VWFA activations across subjects: 1.46 ± 0.22 for words, 2.03 ± 0.28 for nonwords; p<0.005, signed-rank test across 17 subject activations).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of VWFA activations.

claim: VWFA activations were similar for transposed nonwords compared to substituted words.
source: However, activations were similar for transposed nonwords compared to substituted words (mean ±std VWFA activations across subjects: 1.42 ± 0.33 for transposed nonwords, 1.38 ± 0.33 for substituted nonwords; p=0.62, signed-rank test).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of VWFA activations.

claim: Lexical decisions are driven by the VWFA.
source: We conclude that lexical decisions are driven by the VWFA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the VWFA activation analysis.

claim: Viewing a string of letters activates a compositional neural code in LO that is subsequently matched with stored word representations in the VWFA.
source: This suggests that viewing a string of letters activates a compositional neural code in LO that is subsequently matched with stored word representations in the VWFA.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined fMRI results.

claim: Existing models of reading assume explicit encoding of letter position and do not account for letter shape.
source: Existing models of reading assume explicit encoding of letter position and do not account for letter shape (Gomez et al., 2008; Davis, 2010; Norris and Kinoshita, 2012; Norris, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The compositional letter code encodes letter shape explicitly and position implicitly through asymmetric spatial summation.
source: By contrast, our model encodes letter shape explicitly and position implicitly through asymmetric spatial summation.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the proposed model.

claim: The implicit coding of letter position avoids the complication of counting transpositions.
source: The implicit coding of letter position avoids the complication of counting transpositions (Yarkoni et al., 2008; Yap et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an advantage of the model supported by citations.

claim: The compositional letter code is neurally plausible and grounded in well-known principles of object representations.
source: Unlike existing models of reading, our compositional letter code is neurally plausible and grounded in well-known principles of object representations.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's theoretical foundation.

claim: Images that elicit similar activity across neurons in high-level visual cortex will appear perceptually similar.
source: The first principle is that images that elicit similar activity across neurons in high-level visual cortex will appear perceptually similar (Op de Beeck et al., 2001; Sripati and Olson, 2010a; Zhivago and Arun, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The neural response to multiple objects is typically the average of the individual object responses that can be biased toward a weighted sum.
source: The second principle is that the neural response to multiple objects is typically the average of the individual object responses (Zoccolan et al., 2005; Sripati and Olson, 2010b) that can be biased toward a weighted sum (Ghose and Maunsell, 2008; Bao and Tsao, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The letter code assumes no explicit calculations of letter position in a word.
source: Finally, we note that our letter code assumes no explicit calculations of letter position in a word, since the neurons in our model only need to be tuned for retinal position.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model.

claim: Neurons may be tuned not only to retinal position but also to the relative size and position of letters.
source: We speculate that these neurons may be tuned not only to retinal position but also to the relative size and position of letters, as observed in high-level visual cortex (Sripati and Olson, 2010a; Vighneshvel and Arun, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lexical decisions for nonwords are driven by the dissimilarity between the viewed string and the nearest word.
source: We have found that lexical decisions for nonwords are driven by the dissimilarity between the viewed string and the nearest word.
evidence: This is a finding from the lexical decision task.

claim: This idea is consistent with the Interactive Activation model where viewing a string activates the nearest word representation.
source: This idea is consistent with the well-known Interactive Activation model (McClelland and Rumelhart, 1981; Rumelhart and McClelland, 1982), where viewing a string activates the nearest word representation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous models.

claim: The Interactive Activation model does not explain lexical decisions or scrambled word reading.
source: However, the Interactive Activation model does not explain lexical decisions or scrambled word reading, and also does not integrate letter shape and position into a unified code.
evidence: This is a limitation of previous models.

claim: Nonword responses are influenced by the number of orthographic neighbors.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous work showing that nonword responses are influenced by the number of orthographic neighbors (Yap et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Word frequency is a major factor influencing lexical decisions.
source: Likewise, we found word frequency to be a major factor influencing lexical decisions, in keeping with previous work (Ratcliff et al., 2004; Dufau et al., 2012; Yap et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Personal familiarity with words might also influence lexical decisions.
source: We note also that personal familiarity with words, as opposed to the word frequency estimated from text corpora, might also influence lexical decisions (Colombo et al., 2006; Kuperman and Van Dyke, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The compositional shape code provides a quick match to unscramble a word, failing which subjects may initiate more detailed symbolic manipulation.
source: We propose that the compositional shape code provides a quick match to unscramble a word, failing which subjects may initiate more detailed symbolic manipulation.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the study findings.

claim: The success of the letter code challenges the widely held belief that efficient visual processing of letter strings requires higher-order detectors for letter combinations.
source: The success of our letter code challenges the widely held belief that efficient visual processing of letter strings requires higher-order detectors for letter combinations (Grainger and Whitney, 2004; Dehaene et al., 2005; Dehaene et al., 2015; Grainger, 2018).
evidence: This is a claim about the implications of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: The presence of specialized combination detectors should have caused larger model errors for valid words and frequent n-grams, but no such trend was observed.
source: The presence of these specialized detectors should have caused larger model errors for valid words and frequent n-grams, but we observed no such trend (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of model errors shown in Figure 3.

claim: It is possible that there are combination detectors in subsequent stages where multiple letters have to activate single syllables.
source: However, it is possible that there are combination detectors in subsequent stages where multiple letters have to activate single syllables.
evidence: This is speculation about possible higher-level processing.

claim: Reading should increase letter discrimination and increase the asymmetry of spatial summation.
source: Our comparison of upright and inverted bigrams suggests that reading should increase letter discrimination and increase the asymmetry of spatial summation (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is an inference from the upright vs inverted bigram results.

claim: This is consistent with the finding that reading makes words more predictable from letters.
source: This is consistent with our recent finding that reading makes words more predictable from letters (Agrawal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: This is consistent with differences in letter position effects for symbols and letters.
source: It is also consistent with differences in letter position effects for symbols and letters (Chanceaux and Grainger, 2012; Scaltritti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both processes may be driven by visual exposure: repeated viewing of letters makes them more discriminable, while viewing letter combinations induces asymmetric spatial weighting or increased separability.
source: We propose that both processes may be driven by visual exposure: repeated viewing of letters makes them more discriminable (Mruczek and Sheinberg, 2005), while viewing letter combinations induces asymmetric spatial weighting or increased separability.
evidence: This is a proposal supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Perceptual dissimilarities between strings matched best with neural representations in the LO region.
source: First, we found that perceptual dissimilarities between strings, regardless of word/nonword status, matched best with neural representations in the LO region (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: This is consistent with similar findings using letters and natural objects.
source: This is consistent with similar findings using letters (Agrawal et al., 2019) and natural objects (Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Semantic dissimilarities between words matched both with temporal gyrus regions as well as with LO.
source: Second, we have found that semantic dissimilarities between words matched both with temporal gyrus regions as well as with LO (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The finding that temporal gyrus regions match semantic dissimilarities is consistent with these regions participating in the reading network.
source: The former finding is consistent with temporal gyrus regions participating in the reading network (Friederici and Gierhan, 2013), while the latter is concordant with other semantic properties such as animacy encoded in LO (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016; Proklova et al., 2016; Thorat et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The finding that LO matches semantic dissimilarities is concordant with other semantic properties such as animacy encoded in LO.
source: The former finding is consistent with temporal gyrus regions participating in the reading network (Friederici and Gierhan, 2013), while the latter is concordant with other semantic properties such as animacy encoded in LO (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016; Proklova et al., 2016; Thorat et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Whether semantic properties are encoded directly by LO or are a consequence of feedback from language/semantic areas can be distinguished using methods with higher temporal resolution.
source: Whether these semantic properties are encoded directly by LO or are a consequence of feedback from language/semantic areas can be distinguished using methods with higher temporal resolution such as MEG or intracranial recordings.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: There is a striking correlation between lexical decision times for words as well as nonwords in the VWFA.
source: We found a striking correlation between lexical decision times for words as well as nonwords in the VWFA (Figure 5E), suggesting that it is involved in comparing the viewed string with stored words.
evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: VWFA is involved in comparing the viewed string with stored words.
source: We found a striking correlation between lexical decision times for words as well as nonwords in the VWFA (Figure 5E), suggesting that it is involved in comparing the viewed string with stored words.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between VWFA activity and lexical decision times.

claim: The finding that VWFA activity is positively correlated with word response times is consistent with previous studies showing that VWFA activity shows weak activity for frequent words.
source: The finding that VWFA activity is positively correlated with word response times (which reflect word frequency as shown in Figure 4C) is consistent with previous studies showing that VWFA activity shows weak activity for frequent words (Kronbichler et al., 2004; Vinckier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The finding that VWFA activity is correlated with nonword response times is consistent with observations that VWFA is modulated by orthographic similarity to words.
source: The finding that VWFA activity is correlated with nonword response times (which reflect perceptual distance to the corresponding word, as shown in Figure 5E), is consistent with observations that VWFA is modulated by orthographic similarity to words (Vinckier et al., 2007; Baeck et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The finding that VWFA activations were stronger for nonwords compared to words has also been observed recently.
source: Finally, our finding that VWFA activations were stronger for nonwords compared to words (Figure 5E), has also been observed recently (Bouhali et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: The higher activity for nonwords is likely due to many of them being perceptually similar to words, making the lexical decision difficult.
source: While this might seem paradoxical considering its status as a word form area, the higher activity for nonwords is likely due to many of them being perceptually similar to words, making the lexical decision difficult.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the VWFA activation pattern.

claim: VWFA is activated strongly for hard lexical decisions, which is concordant with its higher activation for inverted compared to upright words while making lexical decisions.
source: That VWFA is activated strongly for hard lexical decisions is also concordant with its higher activation for inverted compared to upright words while making lexical decisions (Carlos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Some studies have reported equal activity in VWFA for words and nonwords.
source: Some studies have reported equal activity in VWFA for words and nonwords (Baker et al., 2007), and others have reported higher activity for word-like stimuli (Vinckier et al., 2007; Glezer et al., 2009) – but these observations have been made while subjects performed tasks orthogonal to reading.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There have been surprisingly few studies of VWFA activations during word processing tasks.
source: There have been surprisingly few studies of VWFA activations during word processing tasks (Baeck et al., 2015; Sussman et al., 2018; Bouhali et al., 2019; Carlos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Orthographic (perceptual) similarity between strings was encoded not by VWFA but by LO.
source: By comparing brain activations directly with behavioral responses during a lexical decision task, we found an interesting functional dissociation whereby orthographic (perceptual) similarity between strings was encoded not by VWFA but by LO (Figure 5C) and lexical decisions were encoded by VWFA and not LO (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5F.

claim: Lexical decisions were encoded by VWFA and not LO.
source: By comparing brain activations directly with behavioral responses during a lexical decision task, we found an interesting functional dissociation whereby orthographic (perceptual) similarity between strings was encoded not by VWFA but by LO (Figure 5C) and lexical decisions were encoded by VWFA and not LO (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5F.

claim: Most orthographic processing phenomena are driven by compositional neural representations in LO, rather than by the VWFA.
source: This finding implies that most orthographic processing phenomena are driven by compositional neural representations in LO, rather than by the VWFA.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional dissociation between LO and VWFA.

claim: These findings are consistent with recent intracranial EEG recordings that report a progression from early to late, or letter-level to word-level representations along the ventral occipitotemporal cortex regions.
source: These findings are consistent with recent intracranial EEG recordings that report a progression from early to late, or letter-level to word-level representations along the ventral occipitotemporal cortex regions (Thesen et al., 2012; Hirshorn et al., 2016; Lochy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The letter code's integrated representation of both letter shape and position explains both letter transposition and substitution effects and their relative importance.
source: Its integrated representation of both letter shape and position explains both letter transposition and substitution effects and their relative importance (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The letter code's asymmetric spatial weighting favoring the first letter explains the first-letter advantage observed previously.
source: Its asymmetric spatial weighting favoring the first letter (Appendix 3), explains the first-letter advantage observed previously (Scaltritti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The letter code explains why increasing letter spacing can benefit reading in poor readers.
source: It also explains why increasing letter spacing can benefit reading in poor readers, presumably because it increases asymmetry in spatial summation (Zorzi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Transposing the edge letters results in a bigger change than transposing the middle letters according to the letter model.
source: It can be seen transposing the edge letters (OFRGET) results in a bigger change than transposing the middle letters (FOGRET), thus explaining many transposed letter effects (Norris, 2013).
evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Substituting a dissimilar letter leads to a large change compared to substituting a similar letter according to the letter model.
source: Likewise, it can be seen that substituting a dissimilar letter (FORXET) leads to a large change compared to substituting a similar letter (FORCET).
evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Replacing G with C in FORGET leads to a smaller change than replacing with X, thus explaining how priming is stronger when similar letters are substituted.
source: Replacing G with C in FORGET leads to a smaller change than replacing with X, thus explaining how priming is stronger when similar letters are substituted (Marcet and Perea, 2017).
evidence: This is based on model predictions and supported by citation.

claim: The letter subset FRGT is closer to FORGET than the same letters reversed (TGRF), thereby explaining subset priming.
source: Finally, the letter subset FRGT is closer to FORGET than the same letters reversed (TGRF), thereby explaining subset priming (Grainger and Whitney, 2004; Dehaene et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on model predictions and supported by citations.

claim: The compositional neural code can serve as a powerful baseline for the purely visual shape-based representation triggered by viewing words.
source: We propose that this compositional neural code can serve as a powerful baseline for the purely visual shape-based representation triggered by viewing words, thereby enabling the study of higher order linguistic influences on reading processes.
evidence: This is a proposal about the utility of the model.

claim: Reading sentences is much more complex than reading single words, with potentially many words sampled with each eye movement.
source: Our results constitute an important first step in understanding how we read single words, but reading sentences is much more complex, with potentially many words sampled with each eye movement (Rayner, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Our ability to sample multiple letters or words at a single glance is limited by visual acuity and crowding.
source: Our ability to sample multiple letters or words at a single glance is limited by two factors. The first is our visual acuity, which reduces with eccentricity. The second is crowding, by which letters become unrecognizable when flanked by other letters – this effect increases with eccentricity (Pelli and Tillman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The finding that visual search dissimilarity explains word recognition implies that shape representations are qualitatively similar in the fovea and periphery.
source: Our finding that visual search dissimilarity explains word recognition then implies that shape representations are qualitatively similar in the fovea and periphery.
evidence: This is an inference from the study findings.

claim: The structure of the letter model suggests a possible mechanistic explanation for crowding.
source: Furthermore, the structure of the letter model suggests a possible mechanistic explanation for crowding.
evidence: This is speculation based on the model structure.

claim: Neural responses might show greater sensitivity to spatial location at the fovea compared to the periphery, leading to more discriminable representations of multiple letters.
source: Neural responses might show greater sensitivity to spatial location at the fovea compared to the periphery, leading to more discriminable representations of multiple letters.
evidence: This is speculation about possible neural mechanisms.

claim: Neural responses to multiple letters might be more predictable from single letters at the fovea but not in the periphery.
source: Alternatively, neural responses to multiple letters might be more predictable from single letters at the fovea but not in the periphery.
evidence: This is speculation about possible neural mechanisms.

claim: Both possibilities would predict reduced recognition with closely spaced flankers.
source: Both possibilities would predict reduced recognition with closely spaced flankers.
evidence: This is a prediction from the speculated mechanisms.
